title.narrative: Australia - Indonesia Partnership for Disaster Risk Management

description.narrative: The Australia - Indonesia Partnership for Disaster Risk Management also known as SIAP SIAGA focuses on strengthening humanitarian engagement between Australia and Indonesia and strengthening Indonesia’s management of disaster risks. The program aims to improve Indonesia’s management of disaster risks with a particular focus on strengthening Indonesia’s coordination in preparing for, responding to and supporting recovery from disasters. This program will improve Australia's coordination and collaboration with Indonesia on regional humanitarian preparedness and responses.

description.narrative: Australia helped strengthen Indonesia’s response to health security threats through partnerships with civil society organisations. It supported communities to anticipate, respond, adapt, and recover from the impact of the COVID-19. This included supporting the development of effective communication systems to ensure that information about health security threats was disseminated effectively and efficiently to the public; training for volunteers and establishment of disaster preparedness teams to strengthen the management of health security threats at the community level. The support improved health service provision, increased vaccine uptake including in vulnerable and marginalised groups and increased resilience of vulnerable communities to COVID-19.

Australia provided technical support to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MoHA) and National Disaster Management Authority (BNPB) for the revision of MoHA Regulation No. 46/2008. This revision will clarify and strengthen the role of Local Disaster Management Agencies (BPBD) and is in line with other related regulations , including the minimum service standards on disaster management (MSS-DM). For example, the revised regulation requires all districts to establish a BPBD (previously optional) and upgrade the level of Head of BPBDs to senior management level officers which will strengthen leadership and coordination with other agencies. These revisions also set out requirements for gender mainstreaming and disability inclusion in the DRM sector. The revised regulation will be submitted to Ministry of Law and Human Rights for approval. Once approved, it will become mandatory for sub-national government to implement this in their respective regions.

description.narrative: Australia worked with national and subnational governments to accelerate the implementation of Disaster Resilient Village (Destana), benefiting around 213,522 people (105,810 women and 107,712 men) in 42 villages, across the 3 target provinces. This was achieved by revising the National Destana Guideline and developing a disaster preparedness catalogue system. These products provide operational guidelines required by villages to enhance their resilience by considering the local context. At the provincial level, Australia supported local government to develop a plan to accelerate the achievement of Destana targets. To achieve the above target on Destana, Australia worked with local universities, through their community service (KKN) programs. In NTT, 200 students were involved in Destana activities through the KKN program. East Java province is targeting 70 resilient villages under Destana program this year, exceeding the previous annual targets of 40 resilient villages, with 25 high-risk villages adopting inclusive Destana models.

Australia works with 6 national and 20 subnational organisations of persons with disabilities (OPDs) across its 4 target provinces in the Disaster Risk Management sector. Involving OPDs in policy making processes has increased their understanding of, and participation in, the disaster risk management (DRM) sector. For example, in NTB, Himpunan Wanita Disabilitas Indonesia (HWDI), one of our key OPD partners, reported that their partnership with SIAP SIAGA has improved their knowledge of disaster risk management and strengthened their collaboration with government and other stakeholders in this sector. Previously HWDI was only involved in emergency response, but are now actively involved in policymaking processes and community resilience building through the Disaster Resilient Village (Destana) program. They have also been instrumental in promoting the establishment of Disability Service Units within Disaster Management Offices (BPBD) at provincial and district levels.

Australia works with Palang Merah Indonesia (PMI) to support emergency response work in Indonesia. Learning from the importance of community leadership in disaster response, PMI has strengthened training for its volunteers at the community level in 2023-24, particularly for preparedness, emergency response and post-disaster action. ‍ In the wake of the magnitude 6.5 earthquake in March 2024 near Bawean Island, PMI formed a volunteer team to support the immediate response. The team’s responsibilities included liaising with the community, monitoring and evaluating the operation as well as information dissemination. The team oversaw the distribution of 2,891 meal packages, 200 hygiene and family kits, 300 family tents, 300 blankets, and 1000 jerry cans. ‍ The localised leadership of this team allowed the operation to transition to a community development and capacity-building initiative in the rehabilitation stage, ensuring continuity of benefits long after emergency response stage — and the good work continues to this day. PMI reports that the team remains active and contributes to ongoing village resilience efforts.

Australia, through International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and Indonesian Red Cross (IFRC-PMI), in collaboration with KONSEPSI, a local study and participation development consortium, and the Disaster Risk Reduction Forum of NTB province, initiated a preliminary workshop on Anticipatory Action (AA) - actions taken to reduce the humanitarian impacts of a forecast hazard before it occurs. This workshop was attended by representatives of government and local CSOs, with support from the BPDB (Local Disaster Management Office) of NTB province. It aimed to foster a common understanding on the AA approach among Disaster Risk Management (DRM) stakeholders and establish a commitment to start using AA approaches in practical actions across the DRM cycle. As follow-up, the DRM Forum of NTB province has developed an AA working group to implement the AA Action Plan in the region.

description.narrative: Australia, through International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and Indonesian Red Cross (IFRC-PMI), supported the National Anticipatory Action Working Group to promote the use of an Anticipatory Action (AA) approach for managing hydrometeorological hazards. This work aims to reduce the need for humanitarian response and minimise damage caused by natural disasters. IFRC-PMI assisted the Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Culture and the National Agency for Disaster Management in organising the first National Training-of-Trainers on AA involving 27 NGOs and facilitated by 12 organizations. As a result, 24 champions were certified to conduct capacity-building for sub-national stakeholders and advocate for sustainable funding for AA activities across the country. IFRC-PMI also developed a monitoring dashboard to be used by relevant government agencies to track progress, potential collaborations, and references for AA activities training (please see here https://s.id/aawg-dash).

description.narrative: Australia, through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent (IFRC) and Indonesian Red Cross (PMI) supported the National Anticipatory Action Working Group (AAWG) to promote Anticipatory Action (AA) for hydrometeorological hazards, aiming to reduce humanitarian needs and mitigate climate change impacts. In July 2023, IFRC supported the AAWG in developing a Policy Brief on Early Warning for Early Action to Protect Critical Facilities and Community’s Lives. This advocacy helped the National Agency for Disaster Response (BNPB) to promote the AA approach and incorporate this approach into the National Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMN). IFRC-PMI also supported the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture (KEMENKO PMK) and BNPB in organizing the first National Training for Trainers on AA, involving 27 NGOs and facilitated by 12 organisations. As a result, KEMENKO-PMK certified 24 champions to work on sub-national stakeholder capacity building and advocate on sustainable funding for AA. The AAWG has been successful in integrating AA into Contingency Planning and national funding mechanisms.

During this reporting period, support through the SIAP SIAGA program to both Government and Non-Government organisations to improved inclusion and led to significant policy changes. ‍ At the national level, SIAP SIAGA provided technical assistance to the National Disaster Management Authority (Badan Nasional Penganggulangan Bencana, BNPB) leading to mandating (policy) and widespread adoption (behaviour) of gender-responsive planning and budgeting practices (22 from 24 BNPB directorates adopted this practice in this reporting period). Further, BNPB’s senior leadership formally appointed 10 gender facilitators and 3 gender champions to continue to advance the commitments in the BNPB Gender Roadmap. ‍ At the subnational level, SIAP SIAGA’s support for the establishment of 9 Disability Service Units for Disaster Management also significantly boosted the capacity and leadership of Organisations of Persons with Disabilities (OPDs). OPDs were critical partners in the design and establishment of the Disability Service Units, and SIAP SIAGA provided targeted support to these OPDs to enable them to fulfil this role and advocate for the needs of their members. The support provided has had the added benefit of improving OPDs capacity to interface with government, participate in policy-making and other governance forums – for example, advocating to government for accessible offices and education facilities.

description.narrative: In NTB province, Australia worked with Muhammadiyah Disaster Management Center (MDMC) to enhance community resilience in five target villages. By activating the village’s disaster risk management forums and engaging them in the whole Disaster Risk Management (DRM) process, community members learned to assess their resilience, create action plans, and include this information in village annual planning and budgeting. In Medana village, for example, budget was allocated to support the village resilience team within their village governance system to prepare the village annual work plan, contributing to greater community awareness of disaster risks. This approach expanded their focus beyond emergency response to include the whole spectrum of disaster risk management in the planning cycle. The village resilience team also collected data on people with disability and other vulnerable groups, which is now incorporated in evacuation plans, reflecting their commitment to inclusive disaster preparedness.

description.narrative: In Nusa Tenggara Barat, SIAP SIAGA worked with the Muhammadiyah Disaster Management Center (MDMC) in five villages with 732 direct beneficiaries (181 women and 551 men including 15 persons with disability) on disaster risk management initiatives. ‍ In Desa Medana, North Lombok, initiatives included the installation of evacuation route signs, loudspeakers along the coast for emergency alerts, sea depth markers, and posters in key public areas. Supported by SIAP SIAGA, the Village Disaster Risk Reduction Forum drove this work, building partnerships with organisations to prepare for community-based emergency responses and preparedness activities (such as disaster education) in schools and communities. ‍ Across five villages in NTB, 732 people including women, people with disabilities, and marginalised groups, benefited directly from the program through community-based simulations, targeted outreach by religious leaders, and integration with tourism which strengthened the capacity of local stakeholders in disaster risk reduction. At the end of 2024, a community survey for these villages confirmed increased disaster risk awareness and preparedness. As a result of this support, three villages (Kopang Rembiga, Medana, and Rembitan) allocated funding in their 2025 budgets for disaster mitigation for the first time—embedding resilience into long-term governance.

SIAP SIAGA’s pioneering support for the establishment of nine Disability Service Units for Disaster Management in East Java, Nusa Tenggara Barat and Nusa Tenggara Timur has significantly strengthened the leadership and capacity of Organisations of Persons with Disabilities (OPDs) in disaster management, embedding disability inclusion into local policy-making forums and governance structures. ‍ OPDs played a central role in co-designing the Disability Service Units, defining responsibilities, and participating in decision-making processes. It has deepened OPDs’ understanding of disaster management systems and influenced government partners to institutionalise inclusivity for persons with disabilities and advancing local preparedness while amplifying their voices and leadership. ‍ For example, In East Java, the Indonesian Movement for the Welfare of the Deaf hosted an Inclusive DRR Youth Camp using accessible, simulation-based approaches to raise awareness among deaf communities. It inspired the Provincial Office of Communications to initiate a partnership to deliver digital literacy program comprising 12 training sessions to enhance the digital and economic engagement of persons with disabilities.

description.narrative: The Village Resilience Assessment Tool is a tool that is managed by the National Disaster Management Authority to measure a village’s risk and vulnerability to hazards, including climate-related / hydrometeorological ones. ‍ During the reporting period, SIAP SIAGA promoted the use of this tool to assist villages to plan for climate-related risks, which also increases villages’ resilience to climate-induced hazards. Significant progress was achieved in 42 villages supported by SIAP SIAGA in three Provinces (NTB, NTT, and East Java) in this reporting period: 21 villages moved to Resilient (Madya) status and 21 advanced to Highly Resilient (Utama). A further 38 villages commenced support during this period. ‍ The support through SIAP SIAGA has amplified beyond these 80 villages. In NTB, 26 SIAP SIAGA-trained facilitators supported these assessments in 86 additional villages. In Bali, with endorsement from the Regional Secretary and technical support from SIAP SIAGA, 199 villages in Karangasem and Buleleng conducted self-assessments. The Buleleng District Secretariat took it even further, immediately identifying follow-up actions, resulting in 26 villages allocating funds for disaster risk reduction for the first time.

West Kalimantan Floods Operation: During the emergency period, Australia through the Indonesian Red Cross (PMI), distributed relief items to 44 villages across Ketapang, Sambas, and Bengkayang districts. PMI mobilized 103 personnel from February to March 2024. Distributed items included 3,276 ready meal packages, 14 tonnes of rice, 6,000 litres of bottled water, 58 blankets, 30 baby kits, 30 towels, and food items. Thirty-seven additional personnel were tasked to support the ongoing operations. Natuna Landslide Operation: PMI Natuna mobilized an emergency response team of eight personnel for 14 days. They provided psychological support to 34 people and distributed 25 kitchen sets, 50 blankets, facemasks, and hand-sanitizers. A recovery assessment in August 2023 led to continued services. During this period, PMI established two community-based teams and trained local volunteers. Cash grants totalling AUD 20,828 were distributed to 108 households. GEDSI refresher training was provided to staff, volunteers, and local authorities involved in this response.
